summary.plain_language_summary: Erik, several findings deserve prompt review for Theo: his morning headaches occur alongside a blood pressure reading that a specialist considers high for his age, so please arrange a same-day assessment. His growth record shows much slower height gain than expected and falling height percentiles, alongside increased thirst, nighttime urination, and bedwetting returning. The kidney specialist also noted a creatinine result higher than expected for a child and protein in a urine sample; one set of results cannot establish what is causing these findings. His glucose was normal on that single test, but this does not explain the thirst and urinary changes. His hemoglobin and hematocrit are mildly low by pediatric ranges and may be worth reviewing with his tiredness. The phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase flags use adult ranges and may be normal for a growing child, so they should be interpreted using pediatric ranges.

key_findings.text: The recorded blood pressure of 122/80 was considered high for Theo's age, sex, and height by the nephrology review; it should be confirmed and assessed promptly.
The growth record shows about 2 cm of height gain per year and downward crossing of height percentiles; a planned recheck was missed.
The creatinine of 0.98 mg/dL was considered higher than expected for a school-age child. This is a single result and does not by itself establish kidney function.
The urine was very dilute and had 1+ protein. The sample did not show blood, glucose, or signs of infection.
Hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL and hematocrit 33.1% are mildly below commonly used ranges for a 7-year-old; the available blood count does not identify the cause.
The phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase were flagged using adult ranges, but the endocrinology review notes these values may be within pediatric ranges for a growing child.
The reported glucose of 92 mg/dL is reassuring for that measurement, but does not by itself explain ongoing thirst and nighttime urination.

connections.text: The morning headaches and the blood pressure reading considered high for age should be reviewed together promptly, with the blood pressure rechecked using pediatric standards.

The reported thirst, nighttime urination, and return of bedwetting occur alongside dilute urine and 1+ protein, and are worth reviewing with the history of earlier febrile urinary infections and the missed kidney ultrasound.

The family's observation that clothing and shoe sizes have changed little is consistent with the measured slowing of height gain and falling growth percentiles; this pattern can be considered alongside the urinary symptoms and kidney findings.
Mildly low hemoglobin and hematocrit may be relevant to Theo's tiredness and reduced activity, but the available results do not show the cause or establish a link to the growth or kidney findings.

SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT - FICTIONAL PATIENT - NOT REAL MEDICAL DATA

NORTHSIDE URGENT CARE - VISIT NOTE
Patient: Theo Lindqvist    DOB: 04/02/2019 (7 y)    Visit: 09/20/2026
Clinician: Jordan Kim, PA-C
Accompanied by: father (Erik Lindqvist)

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Headaches for 2 weeks; tired.

HISTORY (per father)
Frontal headaches most mornings for 2 weeks. More tired than usual, less
interested in playing. Drinking a lot of water, waking at night to pass
urine, and two recent bedwetting episodes after being dry for years.
Eating less. No vomiting, no fever, no vision changes, no head injury.

VITAL SIGNS
Temp 36.9 C   HR 92   BP 122/80   RR 20   SpO2 99%
Weight 20.1 kg   Height 116 cm

EXAM
Well appearing, somewhat pale. Neurologic exam normal; no neck stiffness.
Throat and ears normal. Heart and lungs normal.

LABS: Drawn today, see lab report. Alkaline phosphatase and phosphorus
flagged high by the lab; likely normal for a growing child. Hemoglobin
mildly low; suggested iron-rich foods. Kidney function within normal
limits. Urine dilute.

ASSESSMENT
Headache, likely tension-type or viral. Blood pressure within normal
limits.

PLAN
Ibuprofen 200 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for headache.
Encourage fluids. Follow up with pediatrician if not improved in 1 week.
